speaker: Spencer Bryngelson
one_sentence: This lecture introduces competitive PINNs, an adversarial formulation where a discriminator learns to emphasize PINN errors and can achieve much higher PDE-solution accuracy than standard residual-squared PINNs.
core_problem: Standard PINNs train by minimizing a squared PDE residual, but they often plateau around modest accuracy even on benign PDEs. One suspected reason is conditioning: squaring residuals can effectively square already-large condition numbers from PDE discretization, making high-accuracy optimization difficult.
first_principles_model: CPINNs turn PDE solving into a minimax game. The solution network tries to minimize PDE violation, while a discriminator is rewarded for finding where the solution network makes mistakes. The exact PDE solution is an optimal strategy of the zero-sum game. This adversarial weighting changes how errors are penalized and avoids some conditioning pathologies of residual-squared training.
key_claims: PINNs use PDE residuals as loss functions but typically struggle to produce high-accuracy solutions.
Competitive PINNs introduce an adversarial discriminator trained to predict mistakes made by the PINN.
The discriminator and PINN form a zero-sum game whose optimal strategy is the exact PDE solution.
The method avoids squaring large PDE-discretization condition numbers.
On a Poisson problem, CPINNs achieved errors four orders of magnitude smaller than strong PINN baselines.
The approach produced relative errors near single-precision accuracy with consistent epoch-by-epoch decrease.

important_terms.meaning: A neural network trained to satisfy data and governing differential-equation residuals.
An adversarial PINN formulation where a discriminator emphasizes solution errors.
In CPINNs, a learned function rewarded for identifying where the solution network is wrong.
An optimization setting where one player's gain is the other player's loss.
A measure of numerical sensitivity; large values indicate that solving or optimizing may be unstable.

stanford_connections: This talk directly extends the early PINN-failure lectures with a proposed adversarial remedy.
It connects to optimization conditioning as a central explanation for why physics losses can fail.
It also pairs with Neural Galerkin and structure-preserving closure talks as alternative ways to make neural PDE solvers more numerically serious.
practical_caution: Adversarial training can introduce its own stability and tuning challenges. CPINNs should be judged by robust convergence across PDEs, not only by a single favorable benchmark.
selected_evidence: PINNs... currently cannot produce high-accuracy solutions.
Competitive PINNs (CPINNs).
Train a discriminator that is rewarded for predicting mistakes the PINN makes.
Discriminator and PINN participate in a zero-sum game.
Errors four orders of magnitude smaller than the best-performing PINN.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that the form of the physics loss matters. If residual-squared training creates bad conditioning, changing the game can change trainability.

title: Soledad Villar: The Passive Symmetries Of Machine Learning
speaker: Soledad Villar
one_sentence: This lecture explains passive symmetries as invariances induced by arbitrary representation choices, and argues that respecting them can improve machine-learning generalization.
core_problem: Every dataset representation includes investigator choices: coordinates, units, node labels, gauges, or basis conventions. These choices are not part of the data-generating process. A model that depends on them may learn artifacts of representation rather than structure of the phenomenon.
first_principles_model: A passive symmetry is a transformation between equivalent representations of the same underlying object. Coordinate changes, unit conversions, gauge transformations, and graph node permutations should change model inputs and outputs consistently without changing the underlying prediction. Group equivariance is one way to implement this consistency in neural architectures.
key_claims: Representation choices induce exact symmetries because different representations can describe the same object.
Passive symmetries include coordinate freedom, gauge symmetry, units covariance, and permutation symmetry.
These symmetries are external to the data-generating process but affect machine-learning practice.
Some passive symmetries can be implemented as group equivariances.
Respecting passive symmetries is especially valuable for out-of-sample generalization.
The topic connects machine learning practice to ideas from physics and causal modeling.

important_terms.meaning: A symmetry arising from changing representation while leaving the underlying object unchanged.
The fact that the same object or system can be represented in different coordinate systems.
A redundancy in representation where multiple mathematical descriptions correspond to the same physical state.
Consistent transformation of quantities when measurement units are changed.
A model property where transforming the input causes a predictable corresponding transformation of the output.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to equivariant neural networks, graph models, and structure-preserving learning throughout the series.
It also clarifies why symmetries are not just physics decoration; they protect models from arbitrary representation artifacts.
It links to out-of-distribution reliability: generalization improves when models ignore irrelevant choices.
practical_caution: Not every symmetry should be blindly imposed. The model should respect symmetries of representation, but not erase meaningful asymmetries in the underlying data-generating process.
selected_evidence: Any representation of data involves arbitrary investigator choices.
Each choice leads to an exact symmetry.
Passive symmetries... include coordinate freedom, gauge symmetry and units' covariance.
Implemented as group equivariances.
Valuable when the goal... is to generalize out of sample.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that ML models should not depend on arbitrary representational choices. Passive symmetries define what the model must treat as the same.

title: Victor Zavala: Bayesian Optimization With ML Models, Physics, And High-Throughput Experiments
speaker: Victor M. Zavala
organization: University of Wisconsin-Madison / Argonne National Laboratory
one_sentence: This lecture presents Bayesian optimization methods that combine physics reference models, learned residuals, scalable uncertainty estimates, and high-throughput experimental design.
core_problem: Bayesian optimization is attractive when experiments or simulations are expensive, but standard GP-based BO can struggle with large-scale models, physical prior knowledge, and high-throughput experimental settings where many experiments can run in parallel. The problem is how to exploit physics and throughput without losing uncertainty-guided search.
first_principles_model: BO selects the next experiment by optimizing an acquisition function built from a surrogate and uncertainty estimate. If physics provides a reference model, the unknown performance can be decomposed into reference prediction plus residual. Learning the residual with a GP focuses data on what physics misses. The reference model can also partition the design space for parallel search and support scalable acquisition functions for larger parametric models.
key_claims: Bayesian optimization can exploit large-scale ML models, physical knowledge, and high-throughput experiments.
A performance function can be decomposed into a physics-based reference model and a learned residual model.
Learning the residual with a Gaussian process can accelerate search.
Reference models can partition the design space for parallel experimental search.
High-throughput experiments require BO methods that can select batches, not only one point at a time.
Scalable acquisition functions can extend BO to large parametric models with basic uncertainty quantification.

important_terms.meaning: A sample-efficient optimization method using probabilistic surrogates and acquisition functions.
A prior model, often physics-based or low-fidelity, that captures coarse structure of the performance function.
A learned correction for what the reference model fails to predict.
A probabilistic surrogate model that defines a distribution over functions.
A criterion used by BO to choose the next experiment or simulation point.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to active learning, experimental design, and digital-twin calibration across the playlist.
It also complements physics-ML hybrid modeling by treating physics as a prior rather than a replacement for learning.
It provides an optimization-side counterpart to uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling.
practical_caution: A poor reference model can bias the search. Physics-informed BO should monitor residual behavior and uncertainty rather than assuming the reference model is reliable everywhere.
selected_evidence: Bayesian Optimization... exploiting machine learning models, physics and high throughput experiments.
Decomposes the performance function into a reference model... and a residual model.
Learning the residual from data using a Gaussian Process.
Partition the design space and enable parallel search.
Acquisition function.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that BO is controlled experimentation under uncertainty. Physics helps most when it guides search while leaving room to learn its residual errors.

title: Hassan Babaee: CUR Matrix Decomposition For Scalable Reduced-Order Modeling
speaker: Hassan Babaee
one_sentence: This lecture uses CUR matrix decomposition to make time-dependent-basis reduced-order models scalable for nonlinear PDEs while reducing intrusiveness.
core_problem: Dynamical low-rank approximation with time-dependent bases can solve high-dimensional PDEs by evolving a low-rank representation, but generic nonlinear PDEs can destroy the cost advantage. For non-polynomial nonlinearities, evaluating the reduced equations can cost as much as solving the full-order model, and implementation can be highly intrusive.
first_principles_model: DLRA represents a high-dimensional evolving solution with time-dependent low-rank factors. Those factors are updated by minimizing the PDE residual. CUR decomposition selects informative rows and columns to approximate large matrices sparsely, enabling adaptive interpolation of nonlinear terms. This lets time-dependent-basis ROMs approximate generic nonlinear PDEs at their nominal reduced cost.
key_claims: DLRA extracts multidimensional correlations from high-dimensional PDE solutions.
Time-dependent bases evolve from residual minimization rather than being extracted from precomputed data.
DLRA can be efficient for linear or quadratic PDEs, but generic nonlinearities create full-order costs.
Non-polynomial nonlinearities are especially challenging for time-dependent-basis evolution equations.
Adaptive sparse interpolation based on CUR decomposition enables scalable TDB-based ROMs for nonlinear PDEs.
The method reduces the intrusiveness required to apply time-dependent-basis ROMs to new PDEs.

important_terms.meaning: A matrix approximation using selected columns, selected rows, and a small linking matrix.
Approximating an evolving high-dimensional system by time-evolving low-rank factors.
A reduced basis that changes over time rather than being fixed after offline training.
Approximating nonlinear terms by evaluating them at selected informative entries or locations.
A nonlinear term not expressible as a simple polynomial, often complicating reduced evaluation.

stanford_connections: This lecture continues the ROM lineage with a scalable algebraic method for nonlinear PDEs.
It connects to DL-ROMs and adaptive ROMs as another way to make reduced simulation practical.
It also links to active sampling and CUR-style data selection: choose the rows/columns that carry the computation.
practical_caution: Sparse interpolation must control low-rank approximation error. If selected rows or columns miss important nonlinear structure, the reduced model can be fast but inaccurate.
selected_evidence: CUR Matrix Decomposition for Scalable Reduced-Order Modeling.
Dynamical low-rank approximation... high-dimensional partial differential equations.
Time-dependent bases.
Residual minimization.
Adaptive sparse interpolation algorithm based on CUR matrix decomposition.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scalable ROMs need both low-rank structure and cheap nonlinear evaluation. CUR supplies the selective sampling needed to keep nonlinear reduced models reduced.

title: Jian Cao: Physics-Based AI-Assisted Design And Control In Flexible Manufacturing
speaker: Jian Cao
one_sentence: This lecture shows how hybrid physics-based and data-driven methods support design, sensing, prediction, and local control in flexible manufacturing processes such as metal additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming.
core_problem: Flexible manufacturing aims to produce three-dimensional parts without geometry-specific tooling, but the process physics is hard: properties depend on long process histories, geometric features are complex, and the design/control space is high-dimensional. Pure first-principles models can be too slow or incomplete, while purely data-driven models may miss mechanics and control constraints.
first_principles_model: A manufacturing process maps design choices and control inputs through process mechanics into microstructure, material state, shape, and mechanical behavior. Physics supplies conservation, mechanics, and process constraints; machine learning supplies fast prediction, active sensing, and adaptive control. The control target is local and in situ: infer what is happening during the process and adjust inputs before defects become locked into the part.
key_claims: Flexible manufacturing benefits from hybrid physics-based data-driven approaches.
Metal powder-based additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming illustrate production without geometry-specific tooling.
Fundamental process mechanics, process control, and ML can be integrated to predict mechanical behavior during manufacturing.
Machine learning can support active sensing for effective in-situ local process control.
Long history-dependent properties are a central difficulty in manufacturing prediction.
Complex geometries and high-dimensional design spaces make purely manual or brute-force approaches impractical.

important_terms.meaning: Manufacturing methods that can produce varied geometries or products without requiring fixed geometry-specific tooling.
Layer-wise construction of parts, often using metal powder and laser energy in this talk's examples.
A forming process for three-dimensional parts that avoids dedicated dies for each geometry.
Using learned models and measurements to decide what process information to collect during operation.
Control actions taken during manufacturing based on local real-time process information.

stanford_connections: This talk connects industrial digital twins to actual manufacturing control loops.
It also links to active learning and sensing because the model must decide what to measure during the process.
It complements materials microstructure talks by showing how process history creates material behavior.
practical_caution: A manufacturing ML model that ignores process history can miss the real source of material properties. Control needs history-aware state estimation, not just static geometry-to-property prediction.
selected_evidence: Flexible processes... metal powder-based additive manufacturing and rapid dieless forming.
Without geometry-specific tooling.
Integration of the fundamental process mechanics, process control, and techniques including machine learning.
Machine learning for active sensing.
Effective in-situ local process control.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that manufacturing SciML is closed-loop process modeling. Prediction, sensing, and control must be learned around the physics of how parts are made.

title: Matthias Chung: Big Data Inverse Problems
speaker: Matthias Chung
one_sentence: This lecture explains sparse inverse problems at big-data scale and shows how variable projection and neural networks can help choose regularization for stable reconstruction.
core_problem: Inverse problems seek hidden causes from indirect measurements, but they are often ill-posed: many solutions fit the data, noise is amplified, and large data volumes make classical inference expensive. Sparsity helps, but L1-regularized problems introduce difficult choices such as regularization parameters and optimization strategy.
first_principles_model: An inverse problem balances data fidelity with prior structure. Sparsity says the unknown quantity is simple in some vector space or dictionary, so L1 regularization promotes sparse reconstructions. Variable projection reduces coupled optimization by analytically or implicitly eliminating variables, while learned regularization uses DNNs to infer stabilizing hyperparameters from data or problem features.
key_claims: Modern data analytics, ML, and UQ depend on efficient inverse-problem solvers.
Growing model complexity and data volume exceed the limits of many existing inference methods.
Many inverse problems aim to reconstruct quantities with sparse representations.
L1 regularization is widely useful in compressed sensing, dictionary learning, and imaging.
Variable projection provides a new route for sparse inverse optimization.
Deep neural networks can be used to obtain regularization parameters for solving inverse problems.

important_terms.meaning: A problem of inferring unknown causes, fields, or parameters from observed effects.
A problem where solutions may not exist, be unique, or depend stably on the data.
A representation where only a small number of coefficients are nonzero or important.
A penalty on absolute coefficient values that promotes sparse solutions.
An optimization technique that eliminates some variables to reduce or stabilize the remaining problem.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to inverse scattering, adaptive ROMs, and Bayesian calibration across the series.
It also clarifies why regularization is not a tuning afterthought; it is how prior knowledge stabilizes inverse inference.
It links SciML with classical computational mathematics rather than replacing regularization theory.
practical_caution: Learning a regularization parameter does not eliminate the need to understand the prior. A DNN-selected parameter can still encode the wrong bias if the training inverse problems differ from deployment.
selected_evidence: Big Data Inverse Problems... Promoting Sparsity and Learning to Regularize.
Reconstruct quantities with a sparse representation.
Optimization problems with L1 regularization.
A new method based on variable projection.
Deep neural networks (DNNs) to obtain regularization parameters.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that inverse problems need stabilizing assumptions. Sparsity and learned regularization are ways to encode those assumptions at scale.

title: Ameya Jagtap: Scientific Machine Learning Through The Lens Of PINNs
speaker: Ameya Jagtap
one_sentence: This lecture surveys physics-informed neural networks as a SciML framework, emphasizing their capabilities, limitations, scalable variants, and causal time-decomposition strategies.
core_problem: Traditional scientific computing requires known physics, boundary and initial conditions, meshes, and long simulations. PINNs offer mesh-light integration of physics and data, but vanilla PINNs face scaling and trainability limits for big data, large domains, long time horizons, and parameterized PDEs.
first_principles_model: A PINN represents a solution with a neural network and trains it with data and PDE residual constraints. Scalable PINN variants decompose the problem: conservative PINNs enforce conservation across subdomains, extended PINNs split large domains, and causal or temporal sweeping trains time-dependent problems in an order that respects physical causality rather than treating all time points equally.
key_claims: PIML has emerged as an alternative to workflows requiring precise laws, meshes, and long simulations.
PINNs are a central PIML method for solving forward and inverse problems with noisy data.
PINNs have useful capabilities but also important limitations.
Conservative PINNs and extended PINNs are scalable extensions for big data or large models.
Temporal decompositions help scale PINNs over long time horizons.
Causal sweeping provides a unified strategy for training time-dependent PINN problems in physically meaningful order.

important_terms.meaning: Machine learning that incorporates physical laws, constraints, or data from scientific systems.
A neural network trained to satisfy differential-equation residuals and data constraints.
A PINN variant designed to respect conservation laws across decomposed domains.
A domain-decomposition PINN method for scaling to larger or more complex domains.
A training strategy for temporal problems that prioritizes earlier times before later times.

stanford_connections: This lecture synthesizes many early PINN-focused talks: vanilla PINN promise, failure modes, and scalable repairs.
It connects to CPINNs because both try to address limitations of standard residual training.
It also links to operator learning and Neural Galerkin schemes as alternative responses to PINN scaling problems.
practical_caution: PINNs can be effective in selected applications, but the training strategy matters. Large time-domain problems can fail if trained without decomposition, causality, or conservation structure.
selected_evidence: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs).
Current capabilities and limitations of PINNs.
Conservative PINNs (cPINNs) and extended PINNs (XPINNs).
For big data and/or large models.
Causal sweeping strategies for PINNs and their temporal decompositions.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that PINNs are a framework, not one algorithm. Scaling them requires decomposing physics, space, time, and training dynamics.

title: Anima Anandkumar: Neural Operators On Function Spaces
speaker: Anima Anandkumar
one_sentence: This lecture explains neural operators as function-space learners for PDEs and multiscale scientific systems, emphasizing zero-shot generalization and large speedups over numerical solvers.
core_problem: Scientific systems such as weather, climate, deep earth, materials, and quantum-to-planetary-scale processes are governed by mappings between fields, not fixed-size vectors. Standard neural networks tied to one discretization struggle to generalize across resolutions, domains, and boundary conditions.
first_principles_model: A PDE solver maps input functions, such as coefficients, initial conditions, or forcing fields, to output functions, such as solution fields. A neural operator learns this operator directly on function spaces. Because the learned object is a discretization-independent map, it can be evaluated on new meshes and can capture multiscale field-to-field structure more naturally than ordinary finite-dimensional networks.
key_claims: Neural operators are designed for solving PDEs by learning mappings between function spaces.
Function-space learning is especially suitable for multiscale scientific applications.
Applications include weather and climate modeling, deep earth modeling, and other scientific simulations.
Principled neural-operator approaches can enable zero-shot generalization beyond the training domain.
Neural operators can produce 4-5 orders of magnitude speedups over numerical weather models and other simulations.
Their advantage is not just using neural networks, but learning the right mathematical object: an operator.

important_terms.meaning: A neural architecture that learns mappings between functions rather than fixed-dimensional vectors.
A mathematical space whose elements are functions, such as fields over a spatial domain.
Generalizing to new regimes or domains without additional training examples from that regime.
A process whose behavior depends on interactions across many spatial or temporal scales.
Learning the map from inputs to solution functions for a family of problems.

stanford_connections: This talk is a central neural-operator anchor and complements Kaushik Bhattacharya's multiscale operator framing.
It connects to ROMs because both seek reusable fast maps, but operators target function-to-function generalization.
It also links to weather/data-assimilation talks through fast field prediction for atmospheric systems.
practical_caution: Zero-shot generalization must be tested against real distribution shifts, not assumed from architecture alone. Operator learning can still fail outside the training physics or boundary-condition family.
selected_evidence: ML for solving PDEs: neural operators on the function spaces.
Learn mappings between function spaces.
Ideal for capturing multi-scale processes.
Zero-shot generalization beyond the training domain.
4-5 orders of magnitude speedups.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that PDE learning should target solution operators, not isolated solution vectors. The architecture should match the mathematical object.

title: Lori Graham-Brady: ML-Driven Models For Material Microstructure And Mechanical Behavior
speaker: Lori Graham-Brady
one_sentence: This lecture explains how ML can generate realistic material microstructures and learn fast mappings from microstructural images to local stress, strain, damage, and material behavior.
core_problem: Material failure is governed by microstructural features, but real microstructures are random, high-dimensional, and difficult to simulate exhaustively. Experiments may provide limited 2D images, while engineering design needs ensembles of realistic 3D microstructures and rapid property/damage predictions.
first_principles_model: A material's macroscopic mechanical behavior emerges from microstructure. The workflow has two learned components: generate digital microstructures that preserve salient experimental features, and use limited physics-based simulations on those microstructures to train ML surrogates for properties and local fields. Transfer learning can help compare or generate microstructures when handcrafted correlation descriptors are insufficient.
key_claims: Material behavior leading to failure is often tied to microstructural features.
Random microstructural variability creates uncertain material response.
Digital microstructure generation must capture salient experimental features, not only simple n-point correlations.
Translating 2D experimental microstructure images into realistic 3D microstructures is crucial.
Transfer learning can support rapid generation or comparison of different microstructure families.
ML models can map microstructural images to properties and local stress, strain, and damage fields orders of magnitude faster than physics simulations.

important_terms.meaning: The small-scale internal structure of a material that influences its mechanical behavior.
A microstructure with variability across samples, leading to uncertain material response.
Using learned features from one task or dataset to improve another related task.
Concentration of stress, strain, or damage in particular microstructural regions.
The high-dimensional set of possible material structures, processing choices, and resulting properties.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects materials ML to uncertainty and stochastic mechanics.
It complements manufacturing talks because process and microstructure together determine behavior.
It also links to generative modeling and surrogate acceleration for high-dimensional scientific images.
practical_caution: A generated microstructure is useful only if it preserves the features that control mechanics. Matching visual texture or low-order correlations may not be enough for failure prediction.
selected_evidence: Material behavior leading to failure is often associated with microstructural features.
Random variability of these microstructures leads to uncertain material response.
Digitally generating ensembles of microstructures.
Transfer learning approach to rapid generation of three-dimensional microstructures.
Local stresses, strains and damage accelerate the analyses by orders of magnitude.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that material ML must preserve the microstructural features that drive mechanics. The surrogate is only as good as the generated and simulated microstructure ensemble.

title: Ying Liang: Data-Assisted Algorithms For Inverse Random Source Scattering
speaker: Ying Liang
one_sentence: This lecture presents data-assisted algorithms that use boundary measurements and image-to-image learning to reconstruct statistical properties of random sources in stochastic inverse scattering with fewer realizations.
core_problem: Inverse source scattering appears in antenna synthesis, medical imaging, earthquake monitoring, and related fields. When the source is random and the medium is uncertain, traditional methods may require many realizations and detailed medium coefficients to reconstruct source statistics accurately.
first_principles_model: The physical inverse problem starts from boundary measurements generated by wave or scattering equations. Integral-equation methods provide an initial reconstruction, while data-driven image-to-image algorithms improve it by learning the mapping from measurement-derived approximations to source statistics. The key is not replacing physics but using data to reduce the number of random realizations needed.
key_claims: Inverse random source scattering is a stochastic inverse problem with important applications.
Traditional methods require many realizations and information about medium coefficients.
A data-assisted approach can use boundary measurement data to reconstruct statistical properties of the random source.
Data-driven algorithms can enhance initial approximations obtained from integral equations.
The proposed approach achieved better reconstruction with only one tenth of the realizations needed by traditional methods.
Among tested image-to-image algorithms, pix2pix performed best for well-separated inclusions with accurate positions.

important_terms.meaning: Recovering properties of a source that generated observed scattered waves.
An inverse problem involving random sources, parameters, measurements, or media.
Data collected on the boundary of a domain, used to infer interior properties.
An equation formulation where unknowns appear under integrals, often used in scattering problems.
A conditional image-to-image translation model used here to improve reconstruction maps.

stanford_connections: This talk connects inverse problems, uncertainty, and ML-assisted reconstruction.
It complements Big Data Inverse Problems by showing a specific scattering application with stochastic structure.
It also links to earthquake monitoring and medical imaging as domains where boundary data must reveal hidden sources.
practical_caution: Image-to-image models can improve reconstruction only if their training distribution matches the physics and geometry of the inverse problem. They should be treated as data-assisted corrections, not proof of unique recovery.
selected_evidence: Inverse source scattering problems are essential... antenna synthesis, medical imaging, and earthquake monitoring.
Stochastic inverse problems.
Boundary measurement data to reconstruct the statistical properties of the random source.
Better reconstruction with only 1/10 of the realizations.
The pix2pix method outperforms others.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that data can reduce the sampling burden in stochastic inverse problems when it is anchored to physics-based reconstruction.

title: Paul Atzberger: Generative Machine Learning For Data-Driven Modeling And Reductions
speaker: Paul Atzberger
one_sentence: This lecture surveys generative models for nonlinear dynamical-system reduction, including geometric VAEs for physically meaningful latent representations and stochastic dynamic GANs for probabilistic SDE models.
core_problem: Soft materials, complex fluids, and biophysical simulations involve many spatial and temporal scales plus stochastic fluctuations. Reduced models need to represent nonlinear dynamics and uncertainty, but generic latent-variable models may ignore topology, smoothness, physical principles, and stochastic numerical stability.
first_principles_model: A generative reduction learns a simulator-like representation from observations or high-fidelity simulations. Geometric VAEs impose inductive biases so the latent representation respects topology, smoothness, and physics. SDYN-GANs learn probabilistic dynamics in SDE form, including drift, diffusion, and stable multi-step stochastic integrators. The representation is not just compressed data; it is a learned dynamical model.
key_claims: Generative ML creates opportunities for reduced-order and multiscale modeling of nonlinear scientific simulations.
Physical principles and prior scientific knowledge should be incorporated as inductive biases.
Geometric variational autoencoders can learn representations with topological information, smoothness, and physical adherence.
GD-VAEs can support reductions of high-dimensional dynamical systems and nonlinear PDEs.
SDYN-GANs learn probabilistic dynamical models from observations of stochastic systems.
SDYN-GAN representations use SDEs and stable multi-step stochastic numerical integrators for simulation.

important_terms.meaning: A model that learns to generate samples or trajectories resembling the data distribution.
A VAE designed to preserve geometric, topological, smoothness, or physical structure in the latent representation.
A generative adversarial model for learning stochastic dynamical representations.
A differential equation with random terms that models stochastic dynamics.
A numerical method that advances stochastic dynamics stably across multiple time steps.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects generative modeling with ROMs, stochastic model reduction, and manifold learning.
It complements information-geometry and charting-dynamics talks by emphasizing structure in learned latent spaces.
It also links to UQ because stochastic dynamics require probabilistic reduced models, not just deterministic surrogates.
practical_caution: A generative model can produce plausible trajectories while violating physical laws or stochastic stability. Scientific reductions need structural constraints, not just visual or distributional realism.
selected_evidence: Generative Machine Learning Approaches for Data-Driven Modeling and Reductions.
Incorporate... inductive biases including physical principles.
Geometric Variational Autoencoders... topological information, smoothness, and adherence to physical principles.
Stochastic Dynamic Generative Adversarial Networks (SDYN-GANs).
SDEs and stable m-step stochastic numerical integrators.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that generative SciML should learn structured dynamics, not just samples. The latent space must support simulation.

title: Eduardo Gildin: Guided Deep Learning Manifold Linearization Of Porous Media Flow
speaker: Eduardo Gildin
one_sentence: This lecture presents physics-aware manifold linearization for porous-media flow, using non-intrusive reduction, autoencoders, and Koopman-style lifting for reservoir digital twin operations.
core_problem: Reservoir simulators are expensive because nonlinear porous-media equations require iterative solves at each time step. Digital twin operations need fast closed-loop simulation, optimization, and control, but fully intrusive access to simulator internals is often unavailable or impractical.
first_principles_model: The strategy is to learn a reduced representation where the nonlinear reservoir dynamics behave more linearly. E2CO combines data-driven model reduction and DNNs to match both state trajectories and input-output behavior non-intrusively. A second route augments state space and uses an autoencoder to map reservoir equations to a reduced manifold where a Koopman operator approximates linear evolution, avoiding some nonlinear iteration cost.
key_claims: Reservoir digital twin operations require fast simulation for closed-loop management, drilling, and optimization.
Physics-aware ML can endow proxy models with features related to material balance and conservation laws.
E2CO uses data-driven reduction and DNNs for simultaneous state and input-output matching.
The non-intrusive method does not require access to reservoir simulator internal structure.
POD can be extended by augmenting state space to yield a bilinear system.
Autoencoders can linearize reservoir equations on a reduced manifold through a Koopman-operator view.

important_terms.meaning: Flow through materials with pores, such as oil, gas, or water movement in reservoirs.
A fast computational representation of a reservoir used for monitoring, optimization, and control.
Embed to Control and Observe, a non-intrusive method combining reduction and ML for state and input-output matching.
A linear operator acting on observables of a nonlinear dynamical system.
Learning a transformed low-dimensional representation where nonlinear dynamics become closer to linear.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects Koopman theory, autoencoder ROMs, and industrial digital twins in a reservoir setting.
It also complements learned simulator talks by focusing on non-intrusive deployment alongside existing simulators.
It reinforces the series theme that the useful latent space is one where control and prediction become easier.
practical_caution: A learned linear manifold may work only over the operating envelope represented in the training data. Closed-loop reservoir control needs monitoring for when the latent linearization stops matching the simulator or field data.
selected_evidence: Digital Twin operations for closed-loop reservoir management.
Embed to Control and Observe method (E2CO).
State and input-output matching.
Non-intrusive method does not need to have access to reservoir simulation internal structure.
Linearize the reservoir equations in a reduced manifold by means of a Koopman operator.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a digital twin needs a representation where the control problem is cheap. Manifold linearization is a way to make nonlinear reservoir physics operational.

title: Yexiang Xue: Scaling Up AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
speaker: Yexiang Xue
one_sentence: This lecture tackles computational bottlenecks in AI-driven scientific discovery by embedding differentiable PDE solvers into end-to-end learning and using projection/hash-style acceleration for sparse physics updates.
core_problem: Learning first-principles physics models from experimental data requires a closed loop between data, simulation, gradients, and model discovery. The bottleneck is computational: large-scale PDE simulations are expensive in the forward pass, and backpropagating gradients through them can be even more expensive.
first_principles_model: The proposed view is to treat a PDE solver as a differentiable layer inside a learning pipeline. This lets the model learn PDE structure directly from experimental data while propagating gradients through physics simulation. Scaling then depends on exploiting structure: sparse updates in PDE dynamics, locality in neighbor interactions, and random projection or locality-sensitive hashing to group elements with similar temporal behavior.
key_claims: Closed-loop AI-driven scientific discovery is limited by missing end-to-end frameworks that embed large-scale physics simulation into learning.
Backward gradient propagation through physics models is often more demanding than forward simulation.
PDE solvers can be formulated as fully differentiable neural-network layers.
Differentiable solver layers allow large-scale physics simulations to be embedded into learning workflows.
Locality Sensitive Hashing can accelerate sparse PDE updates by grouping elements with similar neighborhoods.
Random projection and symbolic regression can support efficient discovery of sparse and decomposable PDEs.

important_terms.meaning: A learning loop where model discovery, simulation, and gradient-based optimization are integrated into one differentiable pipeline.
A PDE solver implemented so gradients can be propagated through its computations.
A hashing method that groups similar objects together, used here to exploit similar local PDE neighborhoods.
An update pattern where only a subset of state elements changes in an informative way at each step.
A dimensionality-reduction technique that projects data into a lower-dimensional random subspace while approximately preserving structure.

stanford_connections: This lecture directly connects automatic differentiation, differentiable programming, and PDE discovery.
It also complements neural solver and operator talks by emphasizing scalability of both forward and backward computation.
It extends the equation-discovery thread from symbolic search to differentiable simulation pipelines.
practical_caution: End-to-end differentiable physics can be limited by memory, numerical stiffness, and biased experimental data. Fast gradients are useful only if the embedded solver and discovered PDE remain physically meaningful.
selected_evidence: Lack of end-to-end frameworks embedding large-scale simulation of physics models into learning.
Backward gradient propagation.
PDE solvers are formulated as fully differentiable neural network layers.
Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH).
Sparse updates of PDE models.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scaling scientific discovery requires making physics differentiable and computationally sparse enough to learn from.

title: Dongbin Xiu: Data-Driven Modeling Of Unknown Systems With Deep Neural Networks
speaker: Dongbin Xiu
one_sentence: This lecture presents flow map learning, where deep neural networks approximate the unknown evolution operator behind measurement data and become predictive models for unknown systems.
core_problem: Many dynamical systems are only partially observed: governing equations may be unknown, variables may be missing, parameters may be hidden, and PDE structure may be unavailable. The immediate question is whether one can build a predictive model from the measured time history alone.
first_principles_model: Instead of learning the differential equation directly, flow map learning approximates the evolution operator that maps a current observed state to a future observed state. A DNN is used as a flexible map approximator. Once trained, the learned flow map can predict the observed system and support system analysis, even when the complete state or hidden variables are not known.
key_claims: Predictive modeling of unknown systems can be framed as discovering or approximating the evolution operator behind data.
The evolution operator is the flow map from one system state to another.
Deep neural networks can approximate this flow map from measurement data.
An accurate learned flow map becomes a predictive model for the unknown system.
Flow map learning applies to dynamical systems, missing-variable systems, hidden-parameter systems, and PDEs.
The method can model measured variables even when the full system dimension is unknown.

important_terms.meaning: The operator that maps a system state at one time to its state at a later time.
A map describing how a dynamical system advances through time.
Unobserved state components that influence dynamics but are not measured.
Unknown parameters affecting the system's evolution.
A model used to forecast future system behavior from current or past observations.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to Koopman, charting dynamics, and equation-free modeling as alternative ways to learn evolution from data.
It complements equation discovery by learning the time-advance map rather than explicitly recovering a differential equation.
It also links to reservoir manifold linearization and operator learning because all focus on learning maps.
practical_caution: A flow map learned only on observed variables may hide unresolved memory effects from missing variables. Prediction can work locally but fail when hidden states change the observed dynamics.
selected_evidence: Discover/approximate the unknown evolution operator, i.e., flow map, behind the data.
Deep neural network (DNN) is employed to construct such an approximation.
Serves as a predictive model for the unknown system.
Systems with missing variables and hidden parameters.
Partial differential equations (PDEs).
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a system can be modeled through its time-advance operator even when its governing equations are unknown.

title: Peng Chen: Derivative-Informed Neural Operators
speaker: Peng Chen
one_sentence: This lecture introduces derivative-informed neural operators for PDE-constrained Bayesian inference, experimental design, and stochastic optimization, where both state maps and input derivatives are needed efficiently.
core_problem: Optimization and inference problems governed by large-scale PDEs with high-dimensional random parameters require many expensive PDE solves. Classical methods become prohibitive because each sampling or optimization iteration may need statistical estimates, states, derivatives, and sensitivities.
first_principles_model: A neural operator approximates the map from parameters and controls to a PDE state. For optimization, the derivative of that map with respect to inputs is also crucial. A derivative-informed neural operator trains a reduced-basis architecture to learn both the solution operator and its derivative, reducing the number of expensive PDE solves needed while preserving sensitivity information for downstream algorithms.
key_claims: Large-scale PDE optimization with high-dimensional random parameters appears in Bayesian inverse problems, optimal experimental design, and stochastic optimization.
Classical approaches are computationally prohibitive because statistical measures require many expensive PDE solves.
Derivative-informed neural operators approximate both the PDE state map and derivatives with respect to input variables.
Reduced-basis architectures make the operator scalable to high-dimensional problems.
Only a limited number of training data can achieve high accuracy for both PDE solution and optimization solution.
Derivative information improves the usefulness of neural operators for optimization, not just prediction.

important_terms.meaning: A neural operator trained to approximate both a PDE solution map and its input derivatives.
An inverse problem where unknown parameters are inferred probabilistically from data.
Choosing data-acquisition settings that maximize expected information or utility.
Optimization under uncertainty in parameters, data, or objectives.
A neural architecture that represents outputs in a lower-dimensional basis for efficiency.

stanford_connections: This lecture extends neural operators toward inverse problems and design, where sensitivities matter.
It connects to active subspaces, Bayesian calibration, and differentiable programming because all rely on derivative or sensitivity structure.
It also complements ROM talks by using reduced bases inside operator learning.
practical_caution: A neural operator that predicts states accurately may still be poor for optimization if its derivatives are wrong. Sensitivity validation is essential when the surrogate drives decisions.
selected_evidence: Derivative-informed neural operators.
Approximate not only the mapping... to the PDE state, but also its derivative.
Reduced basis architecture.
Limited number of training data.
Bayesian inverse problems... optimal experimental design... stochastic optimization.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that optimization needs more than fast forward prediction. It needs trustworthy derivatives of the learned physics map.

title: Alvaro Coutinho: Enhancing Data-Driven Workflows For Complex Simulations
speaker: Alvaro Coutinho
organization: Federal University of Rio de Janeiro
one_sentence: This lecture argues that data-driven workflows for large simulations must address I/O bottlenecks by analyzing, reducing, and updating data while simulations run.
core_problem: Complex PDE simulations produce high-dimensional state vectors on fine meshes. Modern compute can generate data faster than storage and I/O systems can write it to disk. If workflows wait until after simulation to save and analyze everything, the data bottleneck can dominate the science.
first_principles_model: A simulation workflow is a coupled computation-and-data pipeline. Data-driven methods such as model discovery, MOR, PINNs, and control need snapshots, but large simulations cannot always export all snapshots. The solution is in situ and on-the-fly analysis: update models during runtime, reduce data before writing, steer simulations, and merge simulation workflows with ML workflows.
key_claims: Data-driven methods are increasingly used in engineering and scientific simulations.
Large transient nonlinear PDE simulations produce high-dimensional data that stress storage systems.
The disparity between compute speed and I/O speed makes it hard to dump large data to disk for later analysis.
Data should be analyzed while the simulation is running or reduced before being saved.
On-the-fly algorithms can update data-driven models as new snapshots arrive.
In situ tools can merge simulation workflows and machine-learning workflows.

important_terms.meaning: Analyzing data while a simulation is running rather than after writing all output to disk.
A performance limit caused by slow data reading and writing relative to computation.
An algorithm that updates during simulation as new data become available.
Compressing or summarizing simulation data to reduce storage and analysis cost.
Changing simulation behavior or analysis choices during runtime based on intermediate results.

stanford_connections: This talk complements all large-scale simulation ML talks by focusing on workflow infrastructure rather than only model architecture.
It connects to ROMs because reduction can happen during simulation to avoid writing full fields.
It also links to industrial SciML deployment: data logistics are part of whether methods work.
practical_caution: If a workflow cannot move data efficiently, a better model will not fix the bottleneck. Scientific ML pipelines must be designed around compute, storage, and I/O constraints.
selected_evidence: One must be cautious regarding I/O operations.
Disparity between computing and I/O speed.
Large simulations to output to disk a large amount of data.
Data should be analyzed while the simulation is running.
Merge... simulation workflow and the Machine learning workflow.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that data-driven simulation is also systems engineering. The model cannot learn from data the workflow cannot afford to move.

title: Thomas Beckers: Physics-Enhanced Gaussian Processes For Electromechanical Systems
speaker: Thomas Beckers
one_sentence: This lecture presents physics-enhanced Gaussian processes, including GP Port-Hamiltonian systems, to learn electromechanical dynamics with uncertainty while remaining physically correct by design.
core_problem: Data-driven models for nonlinear electromechanical systems can be data-hungry and physically inconsistent if they ignore known principles such as energy structure. Penalty-based physics constraints can help but may still permit unphysical models or require significant tuning.
first_principles_model: Gaussian processes provide distributions over functions and uncertainty estimates. Port-Hamiltonian systems encode energy exchange, dissipation, and interconnection structure. GP-PHS combines them by forming a Bayesian distribution over physically structured dynamical systems rather than a single black-box function. Physics-enhanced VAEs extend the idea by putting a GP prior with Green's-function structure on latent dynamics.
key_claims: Data-driven electromechanical models should incorporate basic physical principles for data efficiency and correctness.
Physics-enhanced Gaussian processes provide nonparametric Bayesian learning with uncertainty quantification.
Gaussian Process Port-Hamiltonian systems are physically correct by design rather than by penalty.
GP-PHS uses data to form a distribution over possible Port-Hamiltonian systems.
Physics-enhanced VAEs use physically enhanced GP priors on latent dynamics.
Green's functions can encode linear dynamical prior knowledge in GP kernels.

important_terms.meaning: A Bayesian nonparametric model that defines a distribution over functions.
A dynamics framework that represents energy storage, dissipation, and interconnection.
A model architecture that structurally enforces physics rather than adding physics as a soft penalty.
A function representing the response of a linear system to an impulse, used to encode physics in kernels.
Dynamics occurring in a learned hidden representation, such as the latent space of a VAE.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects uncertainty-aware learning with structure-preserving dynamics.
It complements symplectic and Hamiltonian learning talks by adding Bayesian uncertainty.
It also links to physics-informed kernels and Green's-function perspectives elsewhere in the series.
practical_caution: A physically structured prior is only appropriate if the real system follows that structure. Model mismatch can lead to confident but systematically biased predictions.
selected_evidence: Physics-enhanced Gaussian processes.
Gaussian Process Port-Hamiltonian systems (GP-PHS).
Physically correct by design.
Distribution over all possible Port-Hamiltonian systems.
Green's function... included in the kernel function.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that Bayesian uncertainty and physical structure can be combined in the model class itself, not merely patched on after training.

title: H. S. Udaykumar: Data-Driven Multi-Scale Simulations For Energetic Materials
speaker: H. S. Udaykumar
one_sentence: This lecture describes data-driven multiscale simulation for energetic materials, using ML closures, surrogate models, deep learning, transfer learning, and multifidelity strategies to build structure-property-performance design loops.
core_problem: Energetic material sensitivity and performance depend on physics across nano, micro, meso, and macro scales. Atomistic simulations must inform mesoscale models, and mesoscale models must provide closures for macroscale response. Directly resolving all scales is impossible in practical design loops.
first_principles_model: Materials-by-design requires a structure-property-performance map. Multiscale simulation telescopes physics upward: atomistic mechanisms inform mesoscale localization, mesoscale ensembles define closures, and macroscale models predict performance. Machine learning supplies data-driven closures and surrogates that upscale unresolved localization physics and enable optimization over microstructures.
key_claims: Energetic material sensitivity requires telescoping physics from nano-, micro-, and meso-scales to macro-scale response.
Atomistic simulations must inform mesoscale models, while mesoscale models provide closure to macroscale simulations.
ML algorithms can provide data-driven closures for unresolved subgrid localization physics.
Materials-by-design depends on structure-property-performance relationships.
Surrogate modeling with ensembles of mesoscale calculations is one route to S-P-P design.
Deep learning, transfer learning, and multifidelity modeling can accelerate learning across related energetic materials.

important_terms.meaning: A material that stores and releases chemical energy rapidly, relevant to propellants, explosives, and related systems.
Passing information between models at different physical scales.
A learned model representing unresolved small-scale effects in a larger-scale simulation.
The relationship linking material structure to properties and final performance.
Combining data or simulations of different accuracy and cost levels.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects materials microstructure ML with multiscale closure learning.
It also complements industrial digital-twin and manufacturing talks by focusing on design loops for materials.
It reinforces the closure theme: unresolved physics must be summarized accurately for higher-scale prediction.
practical_caution: Transferring knowledge between energetic materials is useful but risky. Similar material families can still differ in sensitivity mechanisms, so transfer learning needs validation across scales.
selected_evidence: Telescoping physics from the nano- and micro- and meso-scales.
Meso-scale models must provide closure to macro-scale simulations.
Data-driven closures which upscale key (localization) physics.
Structure-property-performance (S-P-P) relationships.
Transfer learning and multi-fidelity modeling strategies.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that materials-by-design is a multiscale closure problem. ML is valuable when it carries the right unresolved physics upward.

title: Amir Arzani: A Flexible And Generalizable XAI Framework For Scientific Deep Learning
speaker: Amir Arzani
one_sentence: This lecture presents an interpretable XAI framework for scientific deep learning that probes trained networks, fits sparse integral-equation models, and improves out-of-distribution reasoning.
core_problem: Scientific deep learning often lacks interpretability and fails under out-of-distribution inputs because training data rarely cover the full feature landscape. Black-box models may predict well in distribution while offering little explanation or extrapolation guidance.
first_principles_model: The framework treats a trained neural network as a source of learned local knowledge. First, probe the network inside the training feature landscape. Then fit an interpretable surrogate from a library of integral equations with kernels and nonlinearities, using sparse regression to select a compact model. This interpretable model can be used by design or post hoc, and resembles a simpler interpretable version of operator learning.
key_claims: Interpretability and generalization are central challenges in scientific deep learning.
OOD inference errors grow because physics-based learning tasks often cannot generate exhaustive datasets.
The proposed XAI framework can be used by-design or post-hoc with black-box models.
The method probes a trained neural network within its trained input landscape.
A sparse library of integral equations is fitted to produce an interpretable model.
The approach relates to neural operators but trades some expressiveness for analytical interpretability.

important_terms.meaning: Methods that make model behavior understandable to humans.
Prediction on inputs outside the distribution represented in training data.
An explanation method applied after a black-box model has already been trained.
A collection of candidate integral-equation forms used to fit interpretable operators.
A regression method that selects a small number of active terms from a larger candidate library.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects explainability with neural operators, Green's functions, and symbolic sparse regression.
It complements Miles Cranmer's scientific-debt talk by offering an equation-like interpretation route.
It also links to OOD reliability, a recurring issue in surrogate models and digital twins.
practical_caution: An interpretable surrogate explains the probed network behavior, not necessarily the true physical system. The explanation should be tested against physical data and governing constraints.
selected_evidence: Lack of interpretability and generalization are key challenges.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inference.
Applied in either by-design or post-hoc fashions.
Library of integral equations.
Sparse regression similar to SINDy.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific explanation can be learned as a sparse operator approximation of a black-box model, but it must still be physically validated.

title: Khalid Jawed: Reduced Order Modeling And Inverse Design Of Flexible Structures
speaker: Khalid Jawed
one_sentence: This lecture uses neural networks and neural ODE ideas to build reduced models for highly deformable structures and to solve inverse design problems for shape-morphing systems.
core_problem: Highly deformable structures involve nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material behavior. Full fine-grained simulations can be expensive, while inverse design for target 3D shapes may require painful trial and error across complex local fabrication or actuation choices.
first_principles_model: A flexible structure may have a lower-dimensional representation that captures its dominant deformation. For a slinky, the helix axis can serve as a reduced state instead of the full helical rod. A neural network trained on Discrete Elastic Rod simulations stores the effective elastic forces in that reduced representation. Neural ODE ideas then let the reduced dynamics be simulated efficiently. For morphing structures, ML maps design or actuation choices to target shapes for inverse design.
key_claims: Highly deformable structures require simulation tools for nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material behavior.
Neural networks can reduce variables and accelerate simulation by orders of magnitude.
A slinky's deformation can often be captured by its helix axis as a reduced-order representation.
Neural networks can store elastic forces in the reduced representation.
Training data can come from fine-grained Discrete Elastic Rod simulations.
Shape-morphing structures motivate inverse design from planar patterns to target 3D shapes.

important_terms.meaning: A structure that undergoes large shape changes requiring nonlinear mechanics.
A lower-dimensional description that captures the dominant structural state.
A neural model representing continuous-time dynamics through differential equations.
A simulation framework for slender elastic structures such as rods, ropes, and helices.
Finding design variables that produce a desired target behavior or shape.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects ROMs, neural ODEs, and inverse design in a tangible mechanics setting.
It also complements manufacturing and materials talks because geometry, fabrication, and mechanics interact.
It reinforces the idea that good reduced variables often come from physical insight, not only from data compression.
practical_caution: A reduced structural coordinate is valid only when it captures the deformation modes used in deployment. If the structure bends, twists, contacts, or buckles outside the training regime, the learned reduced force law may fail.
selected_evidence: Highly deformable structures... nonlinear geometry and nonlinear material.
Reduce the number of variables and speed up the simulation by orders of magnitude.
The axis of the helix is a reduced-order representation.
Neural ordinary differential equations.
Discrete Elastic Rods (DER).
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that inverse design of flexible structures starts with the right reduced mechanical coordinates. ML accelerates the force law once the representation is physically meaningful.

title: Eleni Chatzi: Twinning And Model Discovery For Engineered Systems
speaker: Eleni Chatzi
one_sentence: This lecture frames structural health monitoring and digital twinning as hybrid model-discovery problems where data-driven sensing must be integrated with mechanics to assess, forecast, and act on engineered structures.
core_problem: Modern engineered structures are interconnected, exposed to variable loads, and operated in adverse environments. Basic SHM can detect anomalies, but higher-level tasks such as damage quantification, residual-life prognosis, and preventive action require more than black-box data fitting because the monitored structure must be represented as it is now and under future stressors.
first_principles_model: A structural twin is a live representation of a physical asset. Sparse sensors provide measurements, while mechanics-based models propagate that information to unmeasured locations and future conditions. Model discovery identifies damage, parameters, or structure-state variables that make the model match reality. The twin becomes useful when it can detect, localize, quantify, forecast, and recommend actions.
key_claims: SHM forms a hierarchy: detect damage, localize it, quantify it, and eventually prognose residual life.
Purely data-driven methods are lacking for higher-level SHM tasks such as damage assessment and prognosis.
Digital twins of monitored structures require physics-based representations grounded in mechanics.
Hybrid SHM can represent a structure as-is rather than only as-designed.
Augmented twin representations can anticipate performance under future stressors.
A useful twin should advise preventive and remedial actions, not only visualize measurements.

important_terms.meaning: Sensing and modeling methods for detecting, localizing, quantifying, and prognosing damage in structures.
A digital twin enhanced with data-driven updates and physics-based representations of the actual structure.
The remaining useful life of a system before unacceptable degradation or failure.
Estimating structural response across the full object from sparse sensor measurements.
Learning model components, states, or parameters that explain observed structural behavior.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects digital twins, SHM, uncertainty, and model discovery in a deployment-oriented structural setting.
It complements guided-wave SHM by moving from detection/localization toward prognosis and action.
It also links to ROM and surrogate talks because twins need fast but mechanics-aware representations.
practical_caution: A dashboard with sensor data is not a digital twin. Higher-level SHM needs mechanics, uncertainty, and future-load reasoning before it can support maintenance decisions.
selected_evidence: SHM comprises a hierarchy... detect, localize and quantify damage.
Offer a prognosis over the system's residual life.
Purely data-driven methods are found to be lacking.
Furnishing a digital twin of a monitored structure.
Augmented twin representations... anticipating performance under future stressors.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that twinning is state estimation plus mechanics plus decision support. Sensors alone do not create a useful twin.

title: Lu Lu: Deep Neural Operators With Reliable Extrapolation
speaker: Lu Lu
one_sentence: This lecture presents DeepONet and related neural-operator extensions for multiphysics and multiscale problems, with special attention to quantifying and improving extrapolation beyond interpolation regimes.
core_problem: Neural operators can learn solution maps for complex systems, but deep learning models are usually strongest in interpolation. Scientific applications need extrapolation across regimes, fidelities, inputs, and coupled physics, where naive operator models may fail silently.
first_principles_model: DeepONet learns nonlinear operators by combining a branch network that encodes input functions and a trunk network that encodes evaluation locations. Extensions adapt this basic operator-learning template to multiphysics, POD-reduced representations, multiple-input operators, Fourier structure, and multifidelity data. Reliable extrapolation requires understanding the complexity of moving outside the training regime and building workflows that detect or reduce that gap.
key_claims: Neural networks can approximate nonlinear operators, not only finite-dimensional functions.
DeepONet learns operators representing deterministic and stochastic differential equations.
DeepM&Mnet extends the operator-learning idea to multiphysics problems.
POD-DeepONet combines proper orthogonal decomposition with operator learning.
MIONet targets multiple-input operators, while multifidelity DeepONet combines data of different cost and accuracy.
Reliable scientific use requires quantifying extrapolation complexity and building workflows for extrapolation.

important_terms.meaning: A deep operator network architecture for learning mappings from functions to functions.
A DeepONet variant that uses proper orthogonal decomposition to reduce output representation.
A neural operator architecture for multiple-input operators.
Learning from data sources with different costs and accuracies.
A measure or characterization of how difficult it is for a model to predict outside its training domain.

stanford_connections: This talk expands the neural-operator thread beyond FNO-style discussions to DeepONet families.
It connects to Anima Anandkumar's operator talk through function-space learning, but emphasizes extrapolation reliability.
It also links to multifidelity, multiscale, and multiphysics themes across the series.
practical_caution: Operator learning does not automatically solve extrapolation. A model can be excellent across sampled functions and unreliable under new physics, scales, or coupled regimes.
selected_evidence: Deep operator network (DeepONet).
DeepM&Mnet for multiphysics problems.
POD-DeepONet.
Multifidelity DeepONet.
Quantify the extrapolation complexity.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that neural operators must be judged by the domain of operators they can reliably generalize across, not just by interpolation error.

title: Krishna Garikipati: Fokker-Planck Inverse Reinforcement Learning
speaker: Krishna Garikipati
one_sentence: This lecture connects inverse reinforcement learning with Fokker-Planck mean-field dynamics to infer both reward and transition functions from observed stochastic trajectories.
core_problem: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer a reward function from observed agent behavior, but conventional IRL usually assumes a known transition function. In many scientific and biological systems, such as cancer cell dynamics, the transition dynamics are not directly accessible and must be inferred along with reward.
first_principles_model: An MDP describes states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and policies. If agent dynamics in state-action space are modeled by SDEs, the corresponding probability density evolves by a Fokker-Planck equation. The lecture proposes an isomorphism between time-discrete Fokker-Planck dynamics and MDP structure, enabling FP-IRL to infer transition, reward, and policy from observed trajectories using variational system identification.
key_claims: IRL estimates an unknown reward function from observed agent trajectories.
Most IRL methods require a transition function that is known or estimated beforehand.
Unknown transition dynamics make scientific IRL significantly harder.
SDE dynamics in state-action space can be represented at the mean-field level by the Fokker-Planck equation.
A time-discrete Fokker-Planck to MDP isomorphism can support physics-aware IRL.
FP-IRL can simultaneously infer transition and reward functions from observed trajectories.

important_terms.meaning: Inferring the reward function that explains observed behavior.
A framework with states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and policies.
A PDE describing the time evolution of a probability density for stochastic dynamics.
The probability rule for moving from one state to another under an action.
Estimating system functions by optimizing a variational or weak-form objective.

stanford_connections: This lecture links stochastic dynamics, inverse problems, and reinforcement learning in a scientific setting.
It complements Fokker-Planck, SDE, and stochastic model reduction themes elsewhere in the series.
It also illustrates a broader motif: using physics structure to make a learning problem identifiable.
practical_caution: Inferring reward from behavior is inherently ambiguous. Physics constraints can reduce ambiguity, but the inferred reward should not be interpreted causally without domain validation.
selected_evidence: Inverse Reinforcement Learning... revealing the rationale underlying the behavior of autonomous agents.
Estimate the unknown reward function... from observed agent trajectories.
IRL needs a transition function.
Fokker-Planck (FP) equation.
Simultaneously infer the transition and reward functions using only observed trajectories.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that behavior inference needs both objective and dynamics. Fokker-Planck structure supplies the missing dynamics side of IRL.

title: Alice Cicirello: Integrating Physics Knowledge In Machine Learning Strategies
speaker: Alice Cicirello
one_sentence: This lecture organizes physics-enhanced machine learning around four biases: observational, inductive, learning, and discrepancy, using friction-force identification as a case study.
core_problem: ML models trained only from data can generalize poorly, extrapolate badly, and produce physically impossible predictions. Engineering problems often have partial physics knowledge, incomplete equations, noisy measurements, and limited data, so the question is how to insert the right physics knowledge into the right part of the learning strategy.
first_principles_model: Physics knowledge can enter ML in different places. Observational bias changes the data by adding or choosing measurements informed by physics. Inductive bias embeds constraints, symmetries, boundaries, or conservation laws into architecture. Learning bias modifies losses, constraints, or algorithms. Discrepancy bias models known gaps between partial equations and observed behavior. Friction identification shows how sparse system ID and GPs can use these biases.
key_claims: Physics knowledge improves small- and medium-data generalization and can enforce consistency with large data.
Data-only ML can suffer observational bias and physically inconsistent predictions.
Observational bias uses physics-informed data sources or augmentation.
Inductive bias embeds prior assumptions such as boundaries, conservation laws, and symmetries into the learning architecture.
Learning bias changes the loss, constraints, or algorithmic procedure.
Discrepancy bias uses partial physics knowledge or known model-form gaps, demonstrated through friction-force identification.

important_terms.meaning: Physics-informed choices about what data are collected, augmented, or emphasized.
A prior restriction built into a model architecture or representation.
Physics information introduced through losses, constraints, or optimization choices.
A modeled correction for known gaps between an imperfect physics model and observations.
Estimating friction forces or laws in a dynamical system from data and physics constraints.

stanford_connections: This lecture provides a useful taxonomy for many earlier talks on physics-informed, physics-guided, and physics-enhanced ML.
It connects to PINNs, sparse system identification, Gaussian-process physics priors, and discrepancy modeling.
It also gives language for deciding where physics should enter a model rather than saying only 'add physics'.
practical_caution: Adding physics knowledge in the wrong bias channel can be ineffective or misleading. For example, a penalty loss may be weaker than an architectural constraint when the physical law must never be violated.
selected_evidence: Four different biases... observational, inductive, learning, and discrepancy.
Poor generalization performance and extrapolation.
Physically inconsistent or impossible prediction.
Friction forces in a dynamical system.
Sparse system identification... Gaussian Processes.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that physics can enter data, architecture, loss, or model discrepancy. Good SciML chooses the insertion point deliberately.

title: Jinlong Wu: Data-Driven Closure Modeling Using Derivative-Free Kalman Methods
speaker: Jinlong Wu
one_sentence: This lecture uses derivative-free Kalman methods to learn deterministic and stochastic closure models for complex dynamical systems from limited and indirect data.
core_problem: Turbulence, cloud dynamics, and other multiscale systems cannot resolve all degrees of freedom. Closure models are necessary, but traditional closures have limited representation power and empirical calibration. Learning closures is harder when data are indirect, limited, or noisy.
first_principles_model: A closure maps resolved variables to the unresolved effects that influence their evolution. Kalman inversion methods treat unknown closure parameters as latent states and update them using ensemble-based data assimilation, without requiring explicit derivatives of the closure objective. This makes it possible to learn closures from indirect observations and to extend from deterministic closures to sparse and stochastic closure forms.
key_claims: Closure problems are critical for complex dynamical systems where resolving all degrees of freedom is infeasible.
Existing closure models remain unsatisfactory partly because of limited representation power and empirical calibration.
Derivative-free Kalman methods can learn closure models from indirect and limited data.
The approach supports deterministic closure learning.
Sparse identification of dynamical systems can also be handled in this framework.
Derivative-free Kalman inversion can learn stochastic closures from indirect data.

important_terms.meaning: A model for unresolved physical effects on resolved variables.
An ensemble-based update method for parameter learning that avoids explicit gradient computation.
Observations that do not directly measure the closure quantity being learned.
Learning governing equations or closures by selecting a small number of active terms.
A closure model that represents unresolved effects probabilistically.

stanford_connections: This lecture continues the closure thread from LES, ROMs, and structure-preserving closure talks.
It connects to data assimilation because Kalman-style updates infer parameters from observations.
It also links to SINDy and sparse system identification as tools for interpretable learned closures.
practical_caution: Derivative-free methods avoid gradients but not identifiability problems. If indirect data are too weak, multiple closure models may explain the observations equally well.
selected_evidence: Closure problems are critical in predicting complex dynamical systems.
Derivative-free Kalman methods.
Learn closure models from indirect and limited amount of data.
Sparse identification of dynamical systems.
Learning of stochastic closures.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that closure learning is inference from partial evidence. Kalman methods provide a gradient-free route when direct closure data are unavailable.

title: Christopher Rackauckas: Generalizing SciML And Differentiable Simulation Beyond Continuous Models
speaker: Christopher Rackauckas
organization: JuliaHub / Pumas AI / MIT Julia Lab
one_sentence: This lecture argues that SciML and differentiable simulation should extend beyond ODEs and PDEs to jump processes, stochastic simulations, agent-based models, particle filters, and differentiable Bayesian computation.
core_problem: Much SciML progress has focused on continuous models such as ODEs and PDEs.
