But scientific simulation also includes discontinuities, stochastic events, agents, particle filters, MCMC, and hybrid model forms. Differentiating these systems introduces mathematical, numerical stability, and implementation challenges that differ from continuous adjoint methods.
first_principles_model: Differentiable simulation means making a simulator trainable with respect to unknown functions or parameters. If a scientific model has unknown components, those functions can be replaced with neural networks or trainable models, provided one can differentiate through the simulation procedure. Generalization beyond continuous models requires differentiating through randomness, events, discrete choices, chaotic trajectories, and inference algorithms.
key_claims: SciML has incorporated ODEs and PDEs into deep learning through differentiable simulation.
Scientific simulation also includes jump diffusions, agent-based models, and other non-continuous forms.
Differentiable simulation can be generalized to chaotic simulations and stochastic simulations.
Particle filters and agent-based models require special differentiation approaches.
Bayesian inverse problems can require differentiating MCMC methods.
As differentiable programming spreads, numerical stability and implementation issues become central.

important_terms.meaning: A simulation implemented so gradients can be computed through it for learning or optimization.
A stochastic process combining continuous diffusion with discrete jump events.
A simulation of many interacting agents following local rules.
A sequential Monte Carlo method for estimating hidden states in stochastic systems.
Gradient-based treatment of Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms or their outputs.

stanford_connections: This lecture broadens the automatic differentiation and differentiable programming thread.
It connects to FP-IRL, stochastic generative models, and Bayesian inverse problems because they require differentiating nonstandard simulation loops.
It also provides a software-infrastructure perspective on making SciML general rather than ODE-only.
practical_caution: A gradient through a stochastic or discrete simulator can be biased, unstable, or implementation-dependent. Differentiability must be matched to the mathematical object being optimized.
selected_evidence: Generalizing scientific learning and differentiable simulation beyond continuous models.
Jump diffusions, agent-based models.
Differentiating stochastic simulations like particle filters.
Differentiation of Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods.
Numerical stability issues, implementation issues.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that SciML must differentiate scientific computation in all its forms, not just smooth ODE/PDE solvers.

title: Elnaz Rezaian: Data-Driven Balancing Transformation For Predictive Model Order Reduction
speaker: Elnaz Rezaian
one_sentence: This lecture reviews balanced truncation and data-driven ERA-style ROMs for predictive control-oriented model reduction, emphasizing error bounds and bottlenecks in large input-output systems.
core_problem: Projection-based ROMs can be fast but may fail in predictive engineering scenarios if they do not preserve input-output behavior or come with error guarantees. Balanced truncation offers system-theoretic guarantees, but analytical and data-driven versions can be expensive for complex systems with many inputs and outputs.
first_principles_model: Balanced truncation identifies states that are both reachable from inputs and observable in outputs, then truncates states that contribute little to input-output behavior. Data-driven variants such as ERA build reduced models from impulse responses or Markov parameters. The resulting ROMs are tailored to control objectives and can have theoretical error bounds, but scaling requires tangential interpolation, output decomposition, and gappy POD-style approximations.
key_claims: Balanced truncation originates from system-theoretic principles and is tailored for control objectives.
Data-driven balancing methods use empirical system Gramians and minimum realization theory.
Theoretical error bounds allow balanced ROMs to operate in truly predictive scenarios.
The eigensystem realization algorithm is a key data-driven balanced truncation method.
ERA can show predictive performance in stiff reactive flow and aero-acoustic systems.
Many input-output channels create computational overhead, motivating tangential interpolation, output decomposition, and low-fidelity gappy POD.

important_terms.meaning: A model reduction method that removes states with low combined reachability and observability.
A matrix measuring reachability or observability properties of a dynamical system.
A data-driven method for constructing reduced state-space models from impulse-response data.
A sequence of impulse-response coefficients used in system realization.
A method for reconstructing or approximating fields from partial observations using POD bases.

stanford_connections: This lecture adds a control-theoretic ROM perspective to the broader model reduction sequence.
It connects to predictive ROMs, inverse design, and digital twins because error bounds matter for deployment.
It also complements CUR and adaptive ROM talks by focusing on input-output balancing rather than only state compression.
practical_caution: A ROM can be low-dimensional and still poor for prediction if it removes states important for outputs or control. Reduction should respect the input-output task, not just state variance.
selected_evidence: Balanced truncation and data-driven variations.
Empirical system Gramians.
Theoretical error bounds.
Eigensystem realization algorithm (ERA).
Gappy POD approach to address this bottleneck.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that predictive ROMs should preserve what the system can be driven to and what can be observed, not merely what has high energy.

title: Michael Glinsky: A Physics-Based ROM Capturing The Topology Of Dynamical Manifolds
speaker: Michael E. Glinsky
one_sentence: This lecture presents a physics-based reduced-order modeling approach inspired by scattering transforms, renormalization ideas, and topology-preserving projections of dynamical manifolds.
core_problem: High-energy-density physics simulations such as pulsed power liner implosions are expensive and nonlinear, yet practical work needs fast surrogates. A ROM that only interpolates state vectors may miss the manifold topology and scale-dependent structure of the dynamics.
first_principles_model: The proposed Heisenberg Scattering Transformation applies a structured deep convolutional transform inspired by Mallat's scattering transform and a Hamiltonian generating functional. It projects dynamics into a renormalization or S-matrix basis where the evolution is constrained to a low-dimensional complex linear subspace. PCA identifies this subspace, and an encoder-decoder MLP quantifies topology through an analytic function on it.
key_claims: The approach is inspired by Mallat's scattering transformation and a canonical Heisenberg-style perspective on dynamics.
A logarithmic generating functional of the Hamiltonian operates on the system state or statistical distribution.
The transform projects dynamics onto a renormalization or scattering-matrix basis.
The low-dimensional complex linear subspace can be identified with PCA.
Topology is quantified using an MLP with decoder/encoder structure approximating an analytic function on the subspace.
The method is applied as a fast surrogate for 2D pulsed power liner implosions, including MagLIF.

important_terms.meaning: A structured wavelet/convolutional transform that builds stable hierarchical representations.
The talk's proposed physics-based transform for representing dynamics in a renormalization/scattering basis.
A basis associated with how physics changes across scale.
The qualitative geometric structure of the low-dimensional manifold on which dynamics evolve.
Magnetized Liner Inertial Fusion, a pulsed-power fusion concept used as an application setting.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects manifold learning, ROMs, topology, and physics-based transforms.
It complements charting dynamics and information geometry by emphasizing that the reduced space has topology, not just coordinates.
It also links to high-energy-density surrogate modeling, where preserving structure matters for fast prediction.
practical_caution: Topology-aware transforms are powerful but specialized. The assumed transform structure must match the physics; otherwise the ROM can preserve the wrong geometric features.
selected_evidence: Physics-based reduced order model capturing the topology of dynamic manifolds.
Scattering Transformation.
Renormalization Basis.
Principal Component Analysis.
Fast surrogate model for 2D pulsed power liner implosions (MagLIF).
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that some ROMs must preserve dynamical topology and scale structure, not just minimize projection error.

title: Mengwu Guo: Probabilistic Methods for Data-Driven Reduced-Order Modeling
speaker: Mengwu Guo
one_sentence: This lecture explains how probabilistic reduced-order modeling can make data-driven digital twins fast while also quantifying uncertainty.
core_problem: Digital twins and multi-query simulations need models that run much faster than full-order solvers. A deterministic surrogate can be fast but overconfident, especially when the online input leaves the region covered by offline simulations.
first_principles_model: A reduced-order model compresses a high-dimensional physical system into a lower-dimensional representation. Probabilistic ROMs add uncertainty to this compression and prediction process. Gaussian process regression treats the full-order solver as an offline black box and builds a simulation-free online surrogate. Deep kernel learning uses neural networks inside manifold Gaussian processes to discover low-dimensional latent dynamics from noisy high-dimensional images. Bayesian operator inference estimates reduced operators from data while retaining the projected reduced-state equation form and embedding regularization and posterior uncertainty.
key_claims: Probabilistic ROMs are useful when fast simulation must also report computational credibility.
Gaussian process reduced-order surrogate modeling uses full-order solvers offline for data generation and avoids simulation online.
Deep kernel learning can combine neural representation learning with Gaussian process uncertainty.
Bayesian reduced-order operator inference is a non-intrusive glass-box method because it estimates reduced operators without requiring full-order solver internals.
Bayesian inference naturally embeds Tikhonov-style regularization and uncertainty quantification.
The three methods span black-box, gray-box, and glass-box levels of access to physics structure.

important_terms.meaning: A reduced-order model that represents uncertainty in predictions, operators, latent states, or model error.
A probabilistic regression method that gives both a mean prediction and predictive uncertainty.
A hybrid method that uses neural networks to learn features or latent coordinates used by a kernel model.
A method for estimating reduced dynamical operators from data using Bayesian priors and posterior uncertainty.
A penalty-based regularization method that stabilizes ill-posed inverse or regression problems.

stanford_connections: This talk connects ROMs, surrogate modeling, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins.
It complements operator inference and neural operator lectures by asking how much physics structure the learner should retain.
It also links to active learning and experimental design because posterior uncertainty can guide where new simulations are most valuable.
practical_caution: A posterior distribution is only as credible as the model class, priors, and training coverage. A simulation-free online surrogate can still fail silently under extrapolation.
selected_evidence: Gaussian process regression.
The online stage is entirely simulation-free.
Bayesian reduced-order operator inference.
A naturally embedded Tikhonov regularization together with a quantification of modeling uncertainties.
Deep kernel learning.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that a useful ROM for deployment should be fast, structurally grounded when possible, and honest about uncertainty.

title: Nicolas Boulle: Elliptic PDE Learning Is Provably Data-Efficient
speaker: Nicolas Boulle
one_sentence: This lecture gives a theoretical explanation for why learning elliptic PDE solution operators can require surprisingly little data.
core_problem: PDE learning often appears data-efficient in practice, but without theory it is hard to know whether this is an accident of benchmarks or a consequence of mathematical structure. The question is why a model can learn an unknown physical solution map from relatively few input-output examples.
first_principles_model: For an elliptic PDE, the object being learned is not one solution but a solution operator: a map from source terms, coefficients, or inputs to solutions. Elliptic operators have smoothing and compactness properties that make their solution maps lower-complexity than arbitrary function-to-function maps. The lecture explains how PDE regularity and randomized numerical linear algebra can be combined to recover these operators with exponential convergence in the number of training examples.
key_claims: PDE learning can be viewed as approximating solution operators between function spaces.
Elliptic PDEs provide structure that makes this operator-learning problem much more data-efficient than generic regression.
The theoretical result explains exponential convergence with respect to training dataset size.
The proof combines prior PDE theory with randomized numerical linear algebra.
The theory may inform better dataset construction and neural operator architecture design.
The result should be read as structure-specific, not as a universal guarantee for all PDE learning.

important_terms.meaning: A class of PDEs, often describing steady-state or equilibrium phenomena, with strong regularity and smoothing properties.
The mapping from a PDE input such as a forcing function to the corresponding solution.
Error reduction that improves exponentially fast as a resource, here training examples, increases.
Algorithms that use random sampling or projections to approximate large matrix and operator computations efficiently.
Mathematical smoothness properties of PDE solutions implied by the equation class and boundary conditions.

stanford_connections: This talk is a theoretical counterpart to neural operator and operator-learning lectures.
It connects sample efficiency to physical structure rather than only to network size.
It also reinforces the recurring theme that the right inductive bias can turn a high-dimensional learning problem into a tractable operator approximation problem.
practical_caution: The guarantee is tied to elliptic PDE assumptions. Hyperbolic, chaotic, discontinuous, or poorly observed systems may not inherit the same data efficiency.
selected_evidence: We aim to approximate solution operators.
We want to reach an exponential convergence rate.
The proof technique combines prior knowledge of PDE theory and randomized numerical linear algebra techniques.
Improving dataset and neural network architecture designs.
PDE learning is provably data-efficient.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that data efficiency often comes from structure in the physical operator, not from the learning algorithm alone.

title: Dimitrios Giannakis: Quantum Information and Data Science for Modeling Classical Dynamics
speaker: Dimitrios Giannakis
one_sentence: This lecture uses ideas from quantum information to generalize operator-theoretic modeling of classical dynamics.
core_problem: Koopman and transfer-operator methods linearize nonlinear dynamics in spaces of observables and densities, but classical formulations usually rely on commutative algebras. The lecture asks what is gained by representing classical dynamics through the richer language of quantum states and non-commutative operator algebras.
first_principles_model: A dynamical system evolves states, but it also evolves observables and probability densities. Koopman operators act on observables, while transfer operators act on densities. The talk reformulates these objects using multiplication operators and density operators, analogous to quantum information. This lets data assimilation and closure be written in a common operator-theoretic framework, with structure-preserving numerical schemes such as positivity-preserving approximation and kernel-based implementation.
key_claims: Koopman and transfer operators enable linear methods for nonlinear dynamics.
Quantum information provides a non-commutative generalization of classical observable and density representations.
Probability densities can be represented as density operators or quantum-state-like objects.
Data assimilation and dynamical closure can be formulated in the same operator-theoretic language.
Positivity-preserving approximations are important because densities and states must remain physically meaningful.
Kernel methods provide a data-driven route to approximating the required operators.

important_terms.meaning: A linear operator that evolves observables of a nonlinear dynamical system.
An operator that evolves probability densities or measures under dynamics.
An operator representation of a statistical state, common in quantum mechanics and used here for classical dynamics.
An algebra where the order of multiplication matters, as with many operators in quantum theory.
A numerical approximation that keeps densities or state representations nonnegative and physically valid.

stanford_connections: This lecture deepens the operator-theoretic thread across Koopman learning, closure modeling, and kernel methods.
It connects physics-informed machine learning with information geometry and quantum-inspired representations.
It also links to climate and geophysical examples through ENSO assimilation and subgrid closure.
practical_caution: The quantum analogy is a mathematical modeling language, not a claim that the classical system is quantum. The value comes from whether the operator representation preserves useful structure and improves computation.
selected_evidence: Koopman and transfer operators.
Density operators.
Positivity-preserving function approximation.
Kernel methods for operator approximation.
Applications to data assimilation and subgrid-scale modeling.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that changing the representation of observables and densities can make nonlinear dynamics look more linear, structured, and computable.

title: Jan Christoph: Predicting Heart Rhythm Disorders from Spatio-Temporal Imaging Data Using AI
speaker: Jan Christoph
one_sentence: This lecture explains how AI can infer hidden cardiac electrical wave dynamics from observable mechanical imaging data.
core_problem: Heart rhythm disorders arise from abnormal electrical waves moving through cardiac tissue, but current imaging cannot easily resolve full three-dimensional electrophysiological dynamics inside the heart wall. Clinicians and scientists need a way to infer dangerous hidden electrical patterns from measurements that are easier to obtain.
first_principles_model: Cardiac cells are electrically excitable nonlinear oscillators. Their coordinated excitation creates reaction-diffusion waves, and those electrical waves trigger mechanical contraction and deformation. If electrical activity leaves a measurable mechanical signature, then a model can learn the inverse map from high-speed fluorescence or ultrasound imaging of deformation back to electrical dynamics. Ex vivo isolated-heart experiments provide paired training data where the hidden electrical state and visible mechanical motion can both be measured.
key_claims: Heart rhythm disorders can be understood as abnormal nonlinear wave activity in cardiac tissue.
Electrical excitation and mechanical deformation are coupled, so mechanics can contain information about electrophysiology.
AI models can learn to predict electrical dynamics from spatiotemporal imaging data.
High-speed fluorescence and ultrasound imaging provide complementary data sources.
Ex vivo isolated-heart training enables supervised learning with paired electrical and mechanical measurements.
The long-term goal is better prediction and understanding of arrhythmia mechanisms.

important_terms.meaning: The study of electrical activity in biological tissue, here cardiac tissue.
A system where local reactions and spatial diffusion combine to create propagating patterns or waves.
Imaging that captures both spatial structure and time evolution.
A medical imaging modality that uses sound waves to observe tissue motion and structure.
Training data collection using organs or tissue outside the living body under controlled experimental conditions.

stanford_connections: This talk connects physics-informed learning, inverse problems, and biomedical imaging.
It mirrors broader DDPS themes where inaccessible states are inferred from observable proxy measurements.
It also links nonlinear waves and reaction-diffusion dynamics to real clinical prediction problems.
practical_caution: A model trained ex vivo may not transfer directly to in vivo clinical settings. Differences in tissue conditions, imaging quality, patient variability, and interventions must be validated carefully.
selected_evidence: Predicting heart rhythm disorders from spatial temporal Imaging data using artificial intelligence.

title: Boris Kramer: Structure-Preserving Learning of High-Dimensional Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Systems
speaker: Boris Kramer
one_sentence: This lecture shows why reduced models of mechanical systems should preserve Lagrangian and Hamiltonian structure rather than only fit trajectories.
core_problem: High-dimensional mechanical systems are expensive to simulate, but naive learned reductions can violate energy, momentum, symmetry, or stability. Such violations may look small over short horizons and then accumulate into poor long-term predictions.
first_principles_model: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics encode dynamics through structured quantities such as energy, momentum, and generalized coordinates. A structure-preserving learning pipeline first reduces dimension and then learns dynamics in coordinates that maintain the relevant mechanical form. By constraining the reduced model to respect this structure, the learner needs fewer examples and obtains more stable, robust, long-horizon predictions than a purely black-box fit.
key_claims: Many scientific and engineering systems are naturally modeled by Lagrangian or Hamiltonian mechanics.
Quantities such as momentum, energy, and vorticity are not just diagnostics; they are part of the system's structure.
Structure-preserving ROMs can be applied to structural mechanics, soft robotics, and wave propagation.
Preserving symmetry or positive definiteness can improve long-term predictive accuracy.
Structured methods can require less training data than non-structured alternatives.
The target is not just low reconstruction error but stable predictive dynamics.

important_terms.meaning: A formulation of mechanics based on kinetic minus potential energy and variational principles.
A formulation of mechanics based on energy and phase-space evolution.
A reduced-order model designed to retain the physical or geometric structure of the original system.
Prediction over horizons where small structural errors can accumulate into large qualitative failures.
A matrix or operator property often tied to stability, energy, and well-posedness.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects geometric mechanics, ROMs, operator learning, and scientific machine learning.
It complements symplectic and physics-informed learning ideas by making conservation and structure central.
It also reinforces the course-wide theme that inductive bias can reduce data requirements.
practical_caution: Structure preservation helps only if the chosen structure matches the system and discretization. Imposing the wrong mechanical form can create false confidence.
selected_evidence: Structure preserving learning of high dimensional lagrangian and hamiltonian systems.
Momentum, energy, vorticity.
Symmetry and positive definiteness is what gives us a long-term predictive accuracy.
Fewer training data than non-structured methods.
Stability, robustness, long-term predictive accuracy.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that in mechanics, respecting the geometry of the equations can matter more than fitting the next state.

title: Z. Zhang: DeepParticle: Learning Invariant Measure by a Deep Neural Network Minimizing Wasserstein Distance
speaker: Z. Zhang
one_sentence: This lecture presents DeepParticle, a method that learns parameterized invariant measures for high-dimensional PDE-related particle dynamics.
core_problem: High-dimensional PDEs with fronts, sharp gradients, or concentrations are difficult for mesh methods, while mesh-free interacting-particle methods can become expensive for long-time resolved computation. The challenge is to predict behavior at costly physical regimes without running the full particle computation there.
first_principles_model: For Fisher-KPP front speeds in incompressible flows, PDE analysis reduces the target quantity to the principal eigenvalue of an advection-diffusion operator. A Feynman-Kac stochastic representation enables a genetic interacting-particle algorithm whose distribution converges to a large-time invariant measure. DeepParticle learns a family of these invariant measures, parameterized by the Peclet number, using a physically parameterized neural network and an optimal-transport/Wasserstein objective. Training at moderate Peclet numbers lets the model predict more expensive high-Peclet regimes.
key_claims: DeepParticle integrates deep learning, optimal transport, and interacting particle computation.
The case study focuses on Fisher-KPP front speeds in incompressible flows.
The front-speed computation can be reduced to a principal eigenvalue problem.
The Feynman-Kac formula gives a stochastic representation usable by particle algorithms.
The learned object is a parameterized family of invariant measures.
The method extends toward learning stochastic particle dynamics such as Keller-Segel chemotaxis aggregation.

important_terms.meaning: A method combining neural networks, optimal transport, and interacting particles to learn invariant measures.
A probability distribution that remains unchanged under the long-time evolution of a dynamical or stochastic process.
A representation linking certain PDE quantities to expectations over stochastic processes.
A simulation method that represents distributions using many particles whose dynamics interact or are resampled.
An optimal-transport distance measuring how much mass must move to transform one distribution into another.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects stochastic dynamics, PDE analysis, optimal transport, and deep learning.
It complements talks on operator learning by learning invariant distributions rather than only input-output solution maps.
It also links to rare-event and multiscale simulation because the method targets expensive parameter regimes.
practical_caution: Learning invariant measures at moderate parameters does not automatically guarantee accuracy at extreme parameters. Extrapolation in Peclet number must be checked against physics or higher-fidelity computation.

title: Guang Lin: Towards Third Wave AI: Interpretable, Robust Trustworthy Machine Learning
speaker: Guang Lin
one_sentence: This lecture frames trustworthy scientific AI as a combination of neural operators, uncertainty quantification, physics knowledge, and causal modeling.
core_problem: Scientific and public-health decisions need real-time prediction, surveillance, and defense, but opaque models without uncertainty or interpretability are risky. The question is how to make machine learning robust enough for high-consequence dynamical systems.
first_principles_model: Third Wave AI is presented as a move beyond pure data fitting toward models that combine learning, uncertainty, physics, and causal structure. Neural operator architectures learn mappings between functions while producing uncertainty estimates. Multifidelity, federated, and Bayesian variants let models use data from multiple sources, preserve distributed data constraints, and quantify uncertainty. Physics knowledge and causal discovery help make the resulting models more interpretable and trustworthy.
key_claims: Trustworthy AI requires prediction plus uncertainty, robustness, and interpretability.
Neural operator networks can learn nonlinear operators from functions.
Bayesian neural operators provide simultaneous uncertainty estimates.
Multifidelity and federated architectures address heterogeneous data sources and distributed data constraints.
Physics knowledge can be incorporated to design more interpretable models.
Applications include COVID-19 prediction with uncertainty and causal discovery for Alzheimer's disease.

important_terms.meaning: An AI framing that emphasizes contextual, interpretable, robust, and trustworthy systems rather than black-box pattern recognition alone.
A neural architecture designed to learn mappings between functions or fields.

title: George M. Bollas: Physics-Informed Machine Learning through Symbolic Regression
speaker: George M. Bollas
one_sentence: This lecture shows how symbolic regression can recover interpretable physics models from scarce and noisy data.
core_problem: Many engineering systems need equations, not just predictions, especially when data are scarce, noisy, or needed for diagnosis and prognosis. PINN-style methods can fit PDE constraints, but they may be costly and may not directly reveal the governing model.
first_principles_model: Symbolic regression searches over mathematical expressions to identify compact equations that explain observed data. When combined with automatic differentiation, it can estimate derivatives from time-varying data and search for PDE terms without repeatedly integrating candidate PDEs. Genetic programming can also augment an existing dynamic model with additional symbolic equations that expose how a fault evolves over time.
key_claims: Symbolic regression is useful when the goal is model discovery rather than black-box prediction.
The approach is especially attractive under scarce data.
The presented framework is tested under high noise, including up to 50 percent noise.
Automatic differentiation can remove the need for repeated PDE integration during discovery.
Comparisons with PINNs highlight different tradeoffs between equation discovery and constrained neural fitting.
Fault detection and prognosis benefit from symbolic expressions that describe fault progression analytically.

important_terms.meaning: A search procedure that discovers mathematical expressions fitting data.
An evolutionary search method often used to evolve symbolic expressions or programs.

Predicting how a system fault will progress over time.
